Oura and Dunkin’ Eye Offerings as Wall Street’s IPO Boom Builds
 
Plus, Zohran Mamdani turns his fire on Amazon, and Silicon Valley has a new status symbol
 
 
KAROLIINA PAATOS FOR WSJ
 

1. FROM MY DESK

 

The final weeks of summer are typically quiet on Wall Street. Not this year. A wave of initial public offerings expected after Labor Day is bringing a burst of activity. Fund managers and analysts say their calendars are filling up with meetings with companies eager to test investor appetite. Chief among them is smart-ring maker Oura, targeting a fall listing that could fetch a valuation well above $11 billion. Dunkin’ owner Inspire Brands is looking at an offering as early as the end of this year. Coming on the heels of SpaceX’s $86 billion offering in June—and with AI powerhouse Anthropic waiting in the wings—the U.S. IPO market is on track for a record year. This morning, we look at which companies are lining up to go public—and whether investors are ready to buy.

 

This is an edition of The 10-Point newsletter, a guided tour of the best coverage in The Wall Street Journal. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here. If you’re reading this in your inbox, tap the headline above for online and audio versions of this newsletter.

 
 
 

2. TODAY’S HEADLINES

 

• The Iran war, a conflict President Trump promised would be over within six weeks, is continuing without a clear end in sight nearly six months later.

 

• New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s progressive agenda is putting him on a collision course with Amazon.

 

• Investors are snapping up shabby hotels and whipping them into shape.

 

• The Trump administration is planning what may be the largest mass visa revocation in U.S. history, targeting up to 200,000 foreigners who have applied for asylum status.

 

• Some executives are encouraging employees to swap private Slack messages for public channels so AI agents can scan everyday workplace chatter for key business insights.

• Nvidia’s current financial position looks rock solid to say the least. But the financial engineering it is using to keep revenue growing introduces risks, writes Asa Fitch.

 
 
 

4. READ IT HERE FIRST

 

The world’s craziest stock market has turned into a fright ride.

 

South Korea had the world’s hottest stock market for most of the past year, powered by the AI boom. Driven by memory-chip makers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix—which soared to trillion-dollar valuations—the benchmark Kospi index more than tripled in value. Then came the crash. The Kospi plummeted around 40% over six weeks in June and July, erasing roughly $2.5 trillion in market value. The pain fell hardest on South Korea’s individual investors, known as “ants”—weak individually but capable of collective power. The roller-coaster ride has continued: The Kospi has since rebounded from its low, report Jiyoung Sohn, Sooyoung Rhee and Jack Pitcher.

 

5.

 

Flock cameras are spreading across America. The backlash is growing just as fast.

 

The fight against Flock Safety is getting louder and more sophisticated, even as the company’s AI-enabled cameras continue to spread across America. Flock has 120,000 cameras in 49 states that capture 20 billion license plates a month—along with dents, bumper stickers and other identifying features. The company says it is giving police a powerful tool to catch criminals. But the same bipartisan public anger that has risen up from towns and cities to stall data centers is now aimed at Flock’s spreading camera network. As with data centers, the debate over Flock has spilled into midterm races, from Florida to Rhode Island to San Francisco, reports Kris Maher.

6. SEE THE STORY

 

This high-stakes rematch could decide the House.

Virginia’s Second Congressional District is emerging as a key 2026 battleground as Republican Rep. Jen Kiggans faces former Democratic Rep. Elaine Luria in a rematch. The Virginia Beach contest is widely seen as a bellwether for House control while Republicans face an uphill fight to defend their narrow majority. Contests like this will decide which party holds the House.

8. THE NUMBER

 
22 hours, 14 minutes and 10 seconds
 

That is the world record time to visit every station in the New York City subway system, set in 2023 by speedrunner Kate Jones. Across the globe, transit obsessives spend months dissecting schedules, plotting routes and skipping bathroom breaks to race through urban transit networks in record time—an exacting challenge where a single delayed train can derail months of meticulous planning.

 
 
 

9. AND FINALLY…

 

Silicon Valley’s newest status symbol is a super-rare Sam Altman Swiss watch

 

There are many status symbols in Silicon Valley. Homes with views of San Francisco Bay. Cybertrucks. Also on the list are watches, a staple of titans across industries. OpenAI founder Sam Altman ordered seven custom-designed, OpenAI-branded watches created by Vanguart, a Swiss watchmaker. Modeled after Vanguart’s titanium Orb watch, which starts at $180,000, the timepieces were for select company personnel. Several geeky flourishes were added, including a quote attributed to Altman, “COMPUTE IS DESTINY.”
